newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: New UN proposed budget shows sharp cuts.
newsitem.headline: New UN proposed budget shows sharp cuts.

text.p: Vowing to institute major cuts, the United Nations on Tuesday presented a preliminary two-year budget that showed reductions in expenditures even after inflation.

Joseph Connor, the American undersecretary-general for administration and management, said the proposed 1998-1999 budget was $2.479 billion. Inflation and exchange rates could bring the figures up to $2.583 billion.
The comparative 1996-1997 figure was $2.603 billion in appropriations.
"It's not going to grow. It's going to come down," he told a news conference, adding that future estimates could reduce the figures further.
The United Nations has left vacant 1,182 posts over the past two years. The new budget abolishes 904 of them permanently.
Connor indicated more posts would be eliminated after Secretary-General Kofi Annan announces the reform package in July he promised in response to U.S. pressure to streamline the organisation.

"To supress one-tenth of your work force and to achieve negative nominal growth is a significant achievement," he said. Connor's budget covers about about 8,800 secretariat staff, the main bureaucracy. Other commissions and agencies have separate budgets, most of them funded from voluntary contributions.
But whether the new budget will make any impression on rightwing Republicans in the U.S. Congress is debatable.

The Clinton administration has put most of the funds in its proposed budget that was approved in principle by Congress. But Repubican legislators do not want to appropriate the money until the United Nations has met so-called "benchmarks" on reform.

The Republican conditions, not yet completed, are extensive in both the House and the Senate, with conservatives on both sides producing dozens of them. Many of them would be impossible for the United Nations to fulfil without openly becoming a branch of the U.S. Congress, diplomats say.
The most extreme condition in one bill that would bar any payments and instead credit the United States for voluntary contributions in materials and troops to peacekeeping and refugee efforts.
But Bill Richardson, the U.N. ambassador to the United Nations, said the administration had not begun to fight and denounced all the "doom and gloom" reports.
"There are opening positions that have been illustrated in some of the press reports," he told reporters. "We have votes too. This is going to be a process of peaks and valleys."
